subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.152
textbook_items_in_class.description: Three guavas together weigh 1 kg and are roughly the same size — find each guava's weight as a fraction.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.152
textbook_items_in_class.description: 1 kg of rice packed equally into four packets — find the weight of each packet as a fraction.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 7.1 p.153
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange fraction words (half, quarter, three quarters, one and a quarter, one and a half, two and a half) in ascending order of size.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 7.1 p.152
homework.description: Four friends share 3 glasses of sugarcane juice equally — find each friend's share (Math Talk).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.1 p.153
homework.description: A big fish weighs 1/2 kg and a small fish weighs 1/4 kg — find their combined weight (Math Talk).

time_bands.activity: Open with the roti-sharing dialogue from the textbook: pose the question of why sharing one roti among more children gives each child less. Students discuss in pairs and articulate their reasoning about 1/2 versus 1/4.

Work through Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.152 ("Three guavas together weigh 1 kg and are roughly the same size — find each guava's weight as a fraction.") and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.1 p.152 ("1 kg of rice packed equally into four packets — find the weight of each packet as a fraction.") Students write the fractional unit in each case and compare: which is smaller, 1/3 or 1/4, and why?

Tackle Figure it Out Q5, section 7.1 p.153 ("Arrange fraction words (half, quarter, three quarters, one and a quarter, one and a half, two and a half) in ascending order of size.") Students arrange the words on a hand-drawn strip, then justify the ordering using the principle that a larger denominator in a unit fraction signals a smaller piece.
Class discussion: invite two or three students to state, in their own words, the rule linking denominator size to fraction size. Record agreed wording on the board as a class-generated definition.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight students build here is that the denominator counts equal parts, so more parts means each part is smaller — guard against the misconception that 1/4 > 1/2 because 4 > 2. The roti-sharing context grounds this reasoning before any symbolic work begins. Figure it Out Q3 and Q4 (p.152–153) make excellent home extension for students who finish the ordering task early.

textbook_segments.title: Fractional Units as Parts of a Whole

periods.activity_title: Folding and Naming: From Chikki to Paper Strips

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q(a–h), section 7.2 p.155
textbook_items_in_class.description: Eight chikki pieces are shown; for each, identify what fractional unit of the whole chikki each piece represents (denominators ranging from 4 to 24).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (paper strip folding), section 7.3 p.156
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students fold a paper strip into halves, then quarters, then eighths to generate fractional units 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 and record multiples of each unit in a table.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.158
textbook_items_in_class.description: Continue the table of 1/2 for two more steps (extending repeated addition of 1/2).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.3 p.158
homework.description: Create a similar repeated-addition table for the fractional unit 1/4.

time_bands.activity: Using the chikki context from section 7.2, present Figure it Out Q(a–h), section 7.2 p.155 ("Eight chikki pieces are shown; for each, identify what fractional unit of the whole chikki each piece represents (denominators ranging from 4 to 24).") Students examine the figures and name the fractional unit for each piece, noting that shape may differ but each piece is still one equal part of the whole.

Carry out Activity (paper strip folding), section 7.3 p.156 ("Students fold a paper strip into halves, then quarters, then eighths to generate fractional units 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 and record multiples of each unit in a table.") Each student folds their strip, labels each crease, and writes repeated-addition statements such as 3 × 1/4 = 3/4. Introduce the terms numerator and denominator as the vocabulary for counting fractional units and naming their size.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.158 ("Continue the table of 1/2 for two more steps (extending repeated addition of 1/2).") and share entries aloud, confirming that each row is one more copy of 1/2 added on. Consolidate the idea that a fraction names how many fractional units have been collected.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is reading 3/4 as simply a symbol rather than '3 copies of 1/4' — reinforce the repeated-addition language throughout the strip-folding work. The chikki discussion establishes that equal-sized parts need not be identically shaped, a subtlety worth pausing on before folding begins. Students who complete the table quickly can begin Figure it Out Q2 (p.158) in class.
materials: One long paper strip per student (A4 paper cut lengthwise)
Pencils or markers for labelling folds

periods.activity_title: Building Fractions: Strips, Tables, and Pictures

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 7.3 p.158
textbook_items_in_class.description: Make 1/3 using a paper strip and use it to also make 1/6.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.3 p.158
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw pictures and write addition statements for 5 times 1/4 of a roti and 9 times 1/4 of a roti.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 7.3 p.158
textbook_items_in_class.description: Match each of the four fractional units (1/3, 1/5, 1/6, 1/8) with the correct picture.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q3, section 7.3 p.158 ("Make 1/3 using a paper strip and use it to also make 1/6.") by folding a fresh strip into thirds, then folding one third in half to produce 1/6. They compare the 1/6 strip with a previously made 1/8 strip and discuss which is smaller and why.

Address Figure it Out Q4, section 7.3 p.158 ("Draw pictures and write addition statements for 5 times 1/4 of a roti and 9 times 1/4 of a roti.") Students draw roti circles divided into quarters, shade the required number of parts, and write the corresponding addition and fraction notation. Emphasise the transition from counting fractional units to writing a compact fraction symbol.

Complete Figure it Out Q5, section 7.3 p.158 ("Match each of the four fractional units (1/3, 1/5, 1/6, 1/8) with the correct picture.") Students match, then justify each answer with the denominator-tells-us-the-number-of-equal-parts rule. Brief class share-out to consolidate the numerator–denominator vocabulary.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often struggle to fold an exact third — encourage approximation and discussion rather than demanding precision, since the goal is conceptual. Watch for students who draw 9/4 as nine separate circles rather than as two whole rotis and one partial; address this by connecting the picture to the repeated-addition language built during strip folding. Q5 works well as a quick formative check of whether students can move between symbolic and pictorial representations.

textbook_segments.title: Marking Fraction Lengths on the Number Line

periods.activity_title: Fractions on the Line: Plotting and Discovering Infinity

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.4 p.160
textbook_items_in_class.description: On a number line draw lines of lengths 1/10, 3/10, and 4/5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.4 p.160
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write five fractions of own choice and mark them on the number line (Math Talk).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 7.4 p.160
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many fractions lie between 0 and 1? Think and discuss (Math Talk).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 7.4 p.160
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify the fraction for the length of a black line on a number line where 0–1 is divided into 2 equal parts.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 7.4 p.160
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write fractions giving the lengths of black lines on a number line where 0–1 is divided into 5 equal parts.

time_bands.activity: Draw a number line on the board with 0 and 1 marked. Ask students how they would show 1/3 on it. Guide them to divide the 0–1 segment into three equal parts and label the first mark 1/3, the second 2/3. Extend the discussion to fractions greater than 1 by marking 4/3 and 5/3 beyond the 1-mark.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 7.4 p.160 ("On a number line draw lines of lengths 1/10, 3/10, and 4/5.") and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.4 p.160 ("Write five fractions of own choice and mark them on the number line (Math Talk).") Pairs compare their chosen fractions and check whether they placed them correctly relative to each other.

Class discussion for Figure it Out Q3, section 7.4 p.160 ("How many fractions lie between 0 and 1? Think and discuss (Math Talk).") Students reason that between any two marks one can always divide further, leading to the conclusion that the count is infinite. Record student reasoning on the board.

Students read Figure it Out Q4, section 7.4 p.160 ("Identify the fraction for the length of a black line on a number line where 0–1 is divided into 2 equal parts.") and Figure it Out Q5, section 7.4 p.160 ("Write fractions giving the lengths of black lines on a number line where 0–1 is divided into 5 equal parts.") as a consolidation exercise, writing their answers independently.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is treating the number-line marks as whole numbers and counting intervals rather than equal parts — emphasise that the denominator tells how many equal parts the unit interval is divided into. The infinity discussion in Q3 is a conceptual highlight; allow students to speak before confirming, since the reasoning matters more than a quick answer. Q4 and Q5 serve as a formative check on reading versus constructing number lines.

periods.activity_title: Whole and Part Together: Reading Mixed Fractions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many whole units are in 7/2? (Math Talk)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many whole units are in 4/3 and in 7/3? (Math Talk)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1 (a–c), section 7.5 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Figure out the number of whole units in 8/3, 11/5, and 9/4.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can all fractions greater than 1 be written as mixed numbers? Reason and answer.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3 (a–f), section 7.5 p.162
homework.description: Write six improper fractions (9/2, 9/5, 21/19, 47/9, 12/11, 19/6) as mixed fractions.

time_bands.activity: Draw three number-line diagrams on the board, each marking a fraction greater than 1 (such as 5/3, 7/4, 9/2). Ask students how many whole rotis are contained in each and what remains. Collect responses and establish the idea that an improper fraction carries some whole units plus a leftover fractional part.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 7.5 p.162 ("How many whole units are in 7/2? (Math Talk)") and Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.162 ("How many whole units are in 4/3 and in 7/3? (Math Talk)") in pairs, drawing roti diagrams to support their reasoning. Pairs share their decomposition strategy and the class agrees on a general procedure: divide the numerator by the denominator, quotient = whole units, remainder = leftover fractional units.

Students independently tackle Figure it Out Q1 (a–c), section 7.5 p.162 ("Figure out the number of whole units in 8/3, 11/5, and 9/4.") using the agreed procedure, writing each result as a mixed number.

Discuss Figure it Out Q2, section 7.5 p.162 ("Can all fractions greater than 1 be written as mixed numbers? Reason and answer.") Students justify their answer using the definition: every improper fraction has a quotient and a remainder when numerator is divided by denominator, so yes.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes confuse the whole-number part of a mixed number with the numerator of the remaining fraction — drawing roti diagrams reduces this error. The Math Talk questions are ideal for brief group discussion before written work. Students who complete the exercises early can start Figure it Out Q3 (a–f) (p.162) in class.

periods.activity_title: Converting Both Ways: Improper and Mixed Forms

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3 (a–f), section 7.5 p.162
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write six improper fractions (9/2, 9/5, 21/19, 47/9, 12/11, 19/6) as mixed fractions.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1 (a–f), section 7.5 p.163
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write six mixed numbers (3¼, 7⅔, 9 4/9, 3⅙, 2 3/11, 3 9/10) as improper fractions (Math Talk).

time_bands.activity: Briefly demonstrate on the board the reverse conversion — how 3¼ becomes 13/4 by counting 3 whole units (each made of 4 fourths) plus 1 remaining fourth, giving 12 + 1 = 13 fourths. Ask a student to narrate the steps for a second example, 2⅗, before any written work.

Students complete Figure it Out Q3 (a–f), section 7.5 p.162 ("Write six improper fractions (9/2, 9/5, 21/19, 47/9, 12/11, 19/6) as mixed fractions.") independently, then compare answers with a neighbour. The pair resolves any discrepancy by redrawing the roti diagram for that fraction.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1 (a–f), section 7.5 p.163 ("Write six mixed numbers (3¼, 7⅔, 9 4/9, 3⅙, 2 3/11, 3 9/10) as improper fractions (Math Talk).") For each, they write the multiplication-and-addition statement (e.g., 3 × 4 + 1 = 13, so 3¼ = 13/4) before writing the fraction. A few students share their working on the board.

Quick consolidation: teacher poses one oral improper-to-mixed and one mixed-to-improper conversion for the class to answer on mini-whiteboards or slates, confirming fluency before moving to equivalent fractions.

periods.teacher_notes: The mixed-to-improper direction is often weaker than improper-to-mixed; insist that students write the multiplication-and-addition statement rather than guessing. A common error with cases like 21/19 is to write 1 and 2/19 rather than 1 and 2/19 — check that students treat the remainder correctly as the fractional part over the original denominator. The oral consolidation at the close gives an immediate read on the class's readiness for equivalent fractions.

periods.activity_title: Equal but Different: Building the Fraction Wall

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (fraction wall), section 7.6 p.164
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students make a paper fraction wall using strips divided into halves through sixths and use it to identify equal fractional lengths and equivalent fractions.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1–Q4, section 7.6 p.164
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use the fraction wall to answer four questions about equal fractional lengths (e.g., is 1/2 = 3/6? are 2/3 and 4/6 equivalent? how many 1/6 pieces make 1/2?).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1–Q3, section 7.6 p.165
textbook_items_in_class.description: Three questions using the extended fraction wall: are 3/6, 4/8, 5/10 equivalent? write two equivalent fractions for 2/6; write as many equivalents of 4/6 as possible.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1–Q3, section 7.6 p.166
textbook_items_in_class.description: Three equal-share problems: (1) 3 rotis shared by 4 children — write division, addition, multiplication facts; (2) 2 rotis shared by 4 children; (3) 2 cakes shared by 5 children.

time_bands.activity: Students construct their fraction wall using Activity (fraction wall), section 7.6 p.164 ("Students make a paper fraction wall using strips divided into halves through sixths and use it to identify equal fractional lengths and equivalent fractions.") Each student cuts and folds strips into halves, thirds, fourths, fifths, and sixths, placing them below a 'whole' strip. They then align rows to spot which marks fall directly beneath each other, recording the equalities they observe.

Students answer Figure it Out Q1–Q4, section 7.6 p.164 ("Use the fraction wall to answer four questions about equal fractional lengths (e.g., is 1/2 = 3/6? are 2/3 and 4/6 equivalent? how many 1/6 pieces make 1/2?)") and Figure it Out Q1–Q3, section 7.6 p.165 ("Three questions using the extended fraction wall: are 3/6, 4/8, 5/10 equivalent? write two equivalent fractions for 2/6; write as many equivalents of 4/6 as possible.") using their wall as a physical reference.

Shift to the equal-shares reasoning using Figure it Out Q1–Q3, section 7.6 p.166 ("Three equal-share problems: (1) 3 rotis shared by 4 children — write division, addition, multiplication facts; (2) 2 rotis shared by 4 children; (3) 2 cakes shared by 5 children.") Students explain in writing why doubling the number of children and doubling the rotis does not change each child's share — this is the algebraic principle behind multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number.

periods.teacher_notes: The fraction-wall activity and the equal-shares context provide two independent reasons for the same equivalence rule; pressing students to articulate both explanations deepens reasoning beyond procedural knowledge. A key error to watch for is students claiming that 2/3 = 4/5 because both numerator and denominator increased — insist that the multiplier must be the same for both. Worked examples on lowest terms (p.172–173) are available as a self-study pointer for students who want to read ahead.
materials: Pre-cut paper strips (five or six per student)

periods.activity_title: Same Denominator, Clear Winner: Comparing Fractions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1 (a–c), section 7.6 p.168
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find missing numbers in three equivalent-fraction statements (e.g., 5/4 = ?/8; 4/3 = 12/?; 7/5 = ?/?).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (a–h), section 7.6 p.172
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find equivalent fractions for eight pairs of fractions such that both have the same denominator (e.g., 7/2 and 3/5; 8/3 and 5/6).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (a–d), section 7.6 p.173
textbook_items_in_class.description: Express four fractions in lowest terms: 17/51, 64/144, 126/147, 525/112.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1 (a–e), section 7.7 p.174
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare five pairs of fractions (8/3 vs 5/2; 4/9 vs 3/7; 7/10 vs 9/14; 12/5 vs 8/5; 9/4 vs 5/2) and justify.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2 (a–b), section 7.7 p.174
homework.description: Write two sets of three fractions each in ascending order (7/10, 11/15, 2/5; 19/24, 5/6, 7/12).

time_bands.activity: Students complete Figure it Out Q1 (a–c), section 7.6 p.168 ("Find missing numbers in three equivalent-fraction statements (e.g., 5/4 = ?/8; 4/3 = 12/?; 7/5 = ?/?)") to apply the equivalence rule computationally. Discuss the two-step reasoning: identify the multiplier, then apply it to the missing term.

Work through Figure it Out (a–h), section 7.6 p.172 ("Find equivalent fractions for eight pairs of fractions such that both have the same denominator (e.g., 7/2 and 3/5; 8/3 and 5/6).") and Figure it Out (a–d), section 7.6 p.173 ("Express four fractions in lowest terms: 17/51, 64/144, 126/147, 525/112.") The lowest-terms exercise draws on the method shown in Example (lowest terms 16/20), section 7.6 p.172 and Example (lowest terms 36/60), section 7.6 p.173.

Introduce the comparison method from section 7.7 using Example (compare 4/5 vs 7/9), section 7.7 p.173 ("Compare 4/5 and 7/9 by converting to the common denominator 45: 4/5 = 36/45, 7/9 = 35/45; therefore 4/5 > 7/9.") and Example (compare 7/9 vs 17/21), section 7.7 p.174. Students then tackle Figure it Out Q1 (a–e), section 7.7 p.174 ("Compare five pairs of fractions (8/3 vs 5/2; 4/9 vs 3/7; 7/10 vs 9/14; 12/5 vs 8/5; 9/4 vs 5/2) and justify.") independently.
Quick pair-check: students swap books and verify one comparison each, paying attention to whether the common denominator was formed correctly.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number preserves value, students can now use that principle to compare fractions — name this connection explicitly so students see comparison as an application of equivalence, not a new rule. A frequent error in lowest-terms work is dividing only one of numerator or denominator; Figure it Out (a–d) p.173 will surface this quickly. Example (compare 7/9 vs 17/21) on p.174 is a valuable self-study pointer for students who want an additional demonstration of the method.

periods.activity_title: Ordering and Operating: From Comparing to Adding

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3 (a–b), section 7.7 p.174
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write two sets of four fractions each in descending order (25/16, 7/8, 13/4, 17/32; 3/4, 12/5, 7/12, 5/4).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1 (a–m), section 7.8 p.179
textbook_items_in_class.description: Add thirteen fraction expressions using Brahmagupta's method, including sums of two and three fractions with unlike denominators (e.g., 2/7+5/7+6/7; 3/4+1/3; 2/3+5/6; 9/2+5/4; 9/2+5/4+7/6).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 7.8 p.179
textbook_items_in_class.description: Word problem: Rahim mixes 2/3 litres of yellow paint and 3/4 litres of blue paint — find total volume of green paint.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 7.8 p.179
homework.description: Word problem: Geeta buys 2/5 m and Shamim buys 3/4 m of lace — find total and determine if 1 m border can be covered.

time_bands.activity: Students complete Figure it Out Q3 (a–b), section 7.7 p.174 ("Write two sets of four fractions each in descending order (25/16, 7/8, 13/4, 17/32; 3/4, 12/5, 7/12, 5/4).") using the common-denominator comparison method, ordering all four fractions by first finding a single common denominator for the set.

Open section 7.8 with the chikki-sharing story and the rectangular-strip model showing why 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4. State Brahmagupta's three-step procedure — find common multiple, rewrite each fraction, sum numerators — and demonstrate using Example (add 1/4 + 1/3), section 7.8 p.177 ("Add fractions with unlike denominators using LCM 12: 1/4 = 3/12, 1/3 = 4/12; sum = 7/12.") and Example (add 2/3 + 1/5), section 7.8 p.178.

Students work through a selection of Figure it Out Q1 (a–m), section 7.8 p.179 ("Add thirteen fraction expressions using Brahmagupta's method, including sums of two and three fractions with unlike denominators (e.g., 2/7+5/7+6/7; 3/4+1/3; 2/3+5/6; 9/2+5/4; 9/2+5/4+7/6).") prioritising at least one same-denominator case and two unlike-denominator cases including a three-fraction sum.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q2, section 7.8 p.179 ("Word problem: Rahim mixes 2/3 litres of yellow paint and 3/4 litres of blue paint — find total volume of green paint.") as a brief contextualised application, writing the addition sentence and computing the answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Naming this procedure after Brahmagupta and noting its 628 CE origin adds cultural context and motivates students to engage seriously with it. A common error in three-fraction additions is finding the LCM of only two denominators and then adding the third fraction without rewriting it — insist that all fractions must be rewritten with the common denominator before any numerators are added. Example (add 1/6 + 1/3) on p.179 is a clean self-study pointer for students who benefit from a simpler worked example to revisit.

periods.activity_title: Subtract, Then Discover: History and Fraction Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1 (a–c), section 7.8 p.181
textbook_items_in_class.description: Three same-denominator subtractions: 5/8 − 3/8; 7/9 − 5/9; 10/27 − 1/27.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1 (a–d), section 7.8 p.182
textbook_items_in_class.description: Four unlike-denominator subtractions using Brahmagupta's method: 8/15 − 3/15; 2/5 − 4/15; 5/6 − 4/9; 2/3 − 1/2.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2 (a–c), section 7.8 p.182
textbook_items_in_class.description: Subtract as indicated: 13/4 from 10/3; 18/5 from 23/3; 29/7 from 45/7.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3 (a–b), section 7.8 p.182
textbook_items_in_class.description: Two word problems: (a) Jaya's school is 7/10 km away; she takes an auto for 1/2 km — how far does she walk? (b) Jeevika takes 10/3 min and Namit takes 13/4 min per lap — who is faster and by how much?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This Q1–Q2, section 7.9 p.184
textbook_items_in_class.description: Enrichment puzzle: (1) find three different fractional units that sum to 1; (2) find four different fractional units that sum to 1 (six solutions exist).

time_bands.activity: Demonstrate the rectangular-strip model for subtraction using Example (subtract 6/7 - 4/7), section 7.8 p.180 ("Subtract fractions with same denominator using rectangular strip model: 6/7 - 4/7 = 2/7.") Students then complete Figure it Out Q1 (a–c), section 7.8 p.181 ("Three same-denominator subtractions: 5/8 − 3/8; 7/9 − 5/9; 10/27 − 1/27.") quickly as a warm-up.

Using Example (subtract 3/4 - 2/3), section 7.8 p.181 ("Subtract fractions with unlike denominators using common denominator 12: 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12; difference = 1/12.") as a model, students work through Figure it Out Q1 (a–d), section 7.8 p.182 ("Four unlike-denominator subtractions using Brahmagupta's method: 8/15 − 3/15; 2/5 − 4/15; 5/6 − 4/9; 2/3 − 1/2.") and Figure it Out Q2 (a–c), section 7.8 p.182 ("Subtract as indicated: 13/4 from 10/3; 18/5 from 23/3; 29/7 from 45/7.")

Students solve Figure it Out Q3 (a–b), section 7.8 p.182 ("Two word problems: (a) Jaya's school is 7/10 km away; she takes an auto for 1/2 km — how far does she walk? (b) Jeevika takes 10/3 min and Namit takes 13/4 min per lap — who is faster and by how much?") writing the subtraction sentence and interpreting the answer in context.

Read aloud the brief history in section 7.9, noting the bhinna/bhaga terminology and Brahmagupta's 628 CE codification. Students then attempt Try This Q1–Q2, section 7.9 p.184 ("Enrichment puzzle: (1) find three different fractional units that sum to 1; (2) find four different fractional units that sum to 1 (six solutions exist).") — working in pairs to find the unique three-unit solution (1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6) before exploring four-unit combinations.

periods.teacher_notes: Subtraction with unlike denominators uses exactly the same common-denominator rewriting as addition; students who struggled with addition may need a moment to confirm this symmetry before proceeding. In Q2 (a–c) on p.182, students may confuse 'subtract 13/4 from 10/3' with the order written and reverse the operands — emphasise 'from' as meaning the quantity being reduced. The Try This puzzle in section 7.9 is genuinely open-ended; rewarding students who find even the three-unit solution encourages mathematical exploration beyond computation.

goals.anchor_book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.152
goals.anchor_description: Three guavas together weigh 1 kg and are roughly the same size — find each guava's weight as a fraction.

goals.section_title: Fractional Units as Parts of a Whole
goals.anchor_book_ref: Figure it Out Q(a–h), section 7.2 p.155

items.prompt: One roti is shared equally among 5 children. Which of the following correctly names the fractional unit each child receives?

options.label: A
options.text: 1/5, because the roti is divided into 5 equal parts and each child gets one of those parts

options.label: B
options.text: 1/4, because four cuts are needed to divide a roti into five pieces

options.label: C
options.text: 1/10, because 5 children each need two pieces to feel full

options.label: D
options.text: 5/1, because there are 5 children sharing 1 roti

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — 1/5. The roti is divided into 5 equal parts and each child receives one part, which is the fractional unit 1/5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The denominator of a unit fraction equals the number of equal parts the whole is divided into.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student inverted numerator and denominator, confusing the count of children with the number of equal parts.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student counted the number of cuts rather than the number of equal parts produced.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student introduced an arbitrary assumption about portions rather than reading the fractional unit directly from the equal-share context.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw a circle divided into 5 equal pieces and count them.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a sentence explaining why 1/5 is smaller than 1/3 using only the sharing story.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.1 p.152
exercise.description: Three guavas together weigh 1 kg and are roughly the same size — find each guava's weight as a fraction.

items.section_title: Fractional Units as Parts of a Whole
items.prompt: A square piece of chikki is cut into 8 equal pieces. Each piece is one fractional unit of the whole chikki. A student takes 3 of these pieces. Which statement correctly describes the fraction the student has taken?

options.label: A
options.text: 1/8, because only one fractional unit is named

options.label: B
options.text: 3/8, because 3 pieces each of size 1/8 are collected

options.label: D
options.text: 8/3, because there are 8 pieces and the student took 3

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — 3/8. The student has collected 3 copies of the fractional unit 1/8, which is written as the fraction 3/8.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A fraction counts how many fractional units (1/denominator) have been collected from the whole.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student reversed numerator and denominator, placing total parts in the numerator.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student subtracted the taken pieces from the total rather than naming the collected fraction.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student named only the size of a single piece rather than the total collected.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to look back at the chikki diagrams in section 7.2 and count shaded pieces.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the fraction taken and the fraction remaining, and verify they sum to 1.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q(a–h), section 7.2 p.155
exercise.description: Eight chikki pieces are shown; for each, identify what fractional unit of the whole chikki each piece represents (denominators ranging from 4 to 24).

items.prompt: A paper strip is folded into 4 equal parts. Each part is the fractional unit 1/4. Which repeated-addition statement correctly gives the length of 3 such parts?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. Collecting 3 copies of the fractional unit 1/4 gives the fraction 3/4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A fraction is the result of repeated addition of its fractional unit: 3 × (1/4) = 3/4.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student treated the 3 pieces as a whole-number count separated from the fractional unit rather than integrating them.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student multiplied the fractional units together instead of adding them, confusing repeated addition with repeated multiplication.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added the denominators rather than the numerators, a misconception about how fraction addition works.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the strip-folding table from section 7.3 and identify the row for 3 times 1/4.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the repeated-addition statement for 7 times 1/4 and state whether the result is greater than 1, giving a reason.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.3 p.158
exercise.description: Continue the table of 1/2 for two more steps (extending repeated addition of 1/2).

items.prompt: How many whole units are contained in the improper fraction 11/4?

options.label: D
options.text: 11 whole units, with none left over

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A — 2 whole units with 3/4 remaining. Dividing 11 by 4 gives quotient 2 and remainder 3, so 11/4 = 2 and 3/4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the numerator by the denominator; the quotient gives the whole units and the remainder gives the fractional part.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student used the denominator itself as the whole-unit count rather than dividing numerator by denominator.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student read the numerator directly as the number of whole units, ignoring the denominator entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student computed 11 ÷ 4 as 3 remainder 1, making an arithmetic error (3 × 4 = 12 > 11).

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw 11 quarter-pieces and circle groups of 4 to find whole units.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to convert 11/4 back to an improper fraction from the mixed-number form and verify the round-trip.

exercise.description: How many whole units are in 7/2? (Math Talk)

items.prompt: Section 7.9 describes Brahmagupta's codification of fraction arithmetic. In which year did Brahmagupta write this, and what is one way the Indian fraction tradition reached other parts of the world, according to the section?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Brahmagupta wrote his codification in 628 CE. Indian fraction methods reached Europe via the Arabs, who transmitted Indian mathematical knowledge westward.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the historical facts stated in section 7.9: the date 628 CE and the Arab transmission route.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the section 7.9 text to locate the date and the transmission route.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words what the bhinna or bhaga terminology tells us about how ancient Indian mathematicians thought about fractions.

exercise.description: Enrichment puzzle: (1) find three different fractional units that sum to 1; (2) find four different fractional units that sum to 1 (six solutions exist).

items.prompt: Two groups of children share rotis equally. Group 1 has 3 children sharing 2 rotis. Group 2 has 6 children sharing 4 rotis. Does each child in Group 1 get more, less, or the same as each child in Group 2? Explain your reasoning using what you know about equivalent fractions.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each child gets the same amount. In Group 1 each child gets 2/3 of a roti. In Group 2 each child gets 4/6 of a roti. Since 4/6 = 2/3 (numerator and denominator both multiplied by 2), the two shares are equal. Doubling both the number of children and the number of rotis preserves each child's share.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number produces an equivalent fraction, so 2/3 = 4/6.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to discuss their reasoning with a partner before writing, using the roti-sharing language from section 7.6.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if Group 2 had 7 children sharing 4 rotis instead, would the shares still be equal? Explain using equivalent fractions.

exercise.description: Use the fraction wall to answer four questions about equal fractional lengths (e.g., is 1/2 = 3/6? are 2/3 and 4/6 equivalent? how many 1/6 pieces make 1/2?).

items.prompt: A paper strip represents 1 whole unit. It is folded into 6 equal parts. Write the fraction for 5 of these parts. Then write the repeated-addition statement that shows how this fraction is built from the fractional unit.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each part is the fractional unit 1/6. Five parts give the fraction 5/6. The repeated-addition statement is: 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 5/6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Folding into 6 equal parts gives the fractional unit 1/6; collecting 5 copies gives 5/6 by repeated addition.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw and fold an actual strip or a rectangle on paper to count the parts.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the strip to 9 equal parts and ask the student to write the fractional unit, the fraction for 7 parts, and the repeated-addition statement.

items.section_title: Marking Fraction Lengths on the Number Line
items.prompt: Draw a number line from 0 to 1 and divide the unit interval into 8 equal parts. Mark and label the points 3/8 and 7/8 on your number line. Then write one fraction that lies between 3/8 and 7/8.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The unit interval is divided into 8 equal parts; 3/8 is the third mark from 0 and 7/8 is the seventh mark. Any fraction of the form n/8 where 4 ≤ n ≤ 6 (i.e., 4/8, 5/8, or 6/8) lies between them. For example, 5/8 is a correct answer.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 0–1 into 8 equal intervals and count marks; a fraction between 3/8 and 7/8 has a numerator between 3 and 7 with denominator 8.

inclusivity.support: Provide a pre-drawn number line with 0 and 1 marked so the student only needs to add the eight equal divisions.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a fraction between 3/8 and 7/8 that does not have 8 as a denominator, and justify that it lies in that interval.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 7.4 p.160
exercise.description: On a number line draw lines of lengths 1/10, 3/10, and 4/5.

items.prompt: Convert the improper fraction 17/5 to a mixed number. Then convert the mixed number 4 and 2/7 back to an improper fraction. Show your working for both conversions.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 17/5: divide 17 by 5, quotient 3, remainder 2, so 17/5 = 3 and 2/5. 4 and 2/7: multiply 4 × 7 = 28, add 2 to get 30, so 4 and 2/7 = 30/7.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: To convert improper to mixed: divide numerator by denominator for quotient and remainder. To convert mixed to improper: multiply whole number by denominator and add the numerator.

inclusivity.support: Provide a number line or roti diagram so the student can count whole units in 17/5 visually.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to add 17/5 and 4 and 2/7 as improper fractions using a common denominator and state the result as a mixed number.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3 (a–f), section 7.5 p.162
exercise.description: Write six improper fractions (9/2, 9/5, 21/19, 47/9, 12/11, 19/6) as mixed fractions.

items.prompt: Find the missing number in the equivalent-fraction statement: 3/7 = ?/35. Then express the fraction 24/36 in its lowest terms, showing the common factor you divided by.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3/7 = 15/35 (multiply numerator and denominator by 5, since 7 × 5 = 35, so 3 × 5 = 15). 24/36: the highest common factor of 24 and 36 is 12; 24 ÷ 12 = 2 and 36 ÷ 12 = 3, so 24/36 = 2/3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For missing numerator: identify the multiplier from denominator, apply it to numerator. For lowest terms: divide numerator and denominator by their highest common factor.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student to first find what number multiplies 7 to give 35, then apply the same number to 3.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to demonstrate lowest terms of 24/36 by a step-by-step method (dividing by 2, then 2, then 3) and verify it gives the same answer as dividing by 12 directly.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1 (a–c), section 7.6 p.168
exercise.description: Find missing numbers in three equivalent-fraction statements (e.g., 5/4 = ?/8; 4/3 = 12/?; 7/5 = ?/?).

items.prompt: Arrange the three fractions 5/6, 3/4, and 7/12 in descending order (largest to smallest). Show the equivalent fractions with a common denominator that you used to compare them.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The LCM of 6, 4, and 12 is 12. 5/6 = 10/12; 3/4 = 9/12; 7/12 = 7/12. Comparing numerators: 10 > 9 > 7, so the descending order is 5/6 > 3/4 > 7/12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert all fractions to a common denominator equal to the LCM of their denominators, then compare numerators.

inclusivity.support: Provide a number line from 0 to 1 divided into twelfths so the student can locate each fraction before ordering.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to insert one more fraction between 3/4 and 5/6 and justify its position using the common-denominator method.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3 (a–b), section 7.7 p.174
exercise.description: Write two sets of four fractions each in descending order (25/16, 7/8, 13/4, 17/32; 3/4, 12/5, 7/12, 5/4).

items.prompt: Riya walks 3/5 km to reach a park and then walks a further 3/4 km inside the park. How far does she walk in total? Use Brahmagupta's method to find the answer and express it as a mixed number if applicable.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: LCM of 5 and 4 is 20. 3/5 = 12/20; 3/4 = 15/20. Sum = 27/20. Converting: 27 ÷ 20 = 1 remainder 7, so 27/20 = 1 and 7/20 km. Riya walks 1 and 7/20 km in total.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply Brahmagupta's method: find the LCM of the denominators, rewrite each fraction, add the numerators, then convert to a mixed number.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw a number line and hop 3/5 then 3/4 to see the total is greater than 1, before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the second distance to 7/8 km and ask the student to recompute; then compare the two total distances.
